subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage: I'm Eshaan. At carrom time, Chinmay lost an argument about whether the striker had touched the line. He stamped his foot twice, said “Fine!” and walked out of the room. I expected him to sulk all break. Instead he walked to the end of the corridor and back, twice, with his fists clenched and then loose. Our class rule is that you may take a walk and come back to talk. When he returned, he sat down and said, “I still think it was a foul, but I shouldn't have stormed out.” I couldn't tell how angry he still was.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do twice before walking out?
qa.a: He stamped his foot twice.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling when he stamped and said “Fine!”, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably anger and frustration at losing the argument. He may also have needed to leave before he said something worse, and Eshaan admits not being able to tell how angry Chinmay still was.

qa.q: How did the walk-and-return rule turn the impulse into something safe?
qa.a: It let Chinmay leave and cool down without slamming or shouting, and then return to talk, so the feeling became a boundary and not a fight.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel watching Chinmay walk out?
qa.a: Probably worried or awkward at first, then relieved when Chinmay came back to talk. Eshaan seems to respect the rule.

grounding: A child stamps out after losing an argument and uses a cooling-off walk before returning to talk.

subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage:
Monday: Jahnavi lost the argument about who got the tablet first. She stamped to her room and slammed the door. Her brother Rafiq shouted, “Don't be so dramatic!” and neither spoke at dinner.
Wednesday: Amma sat with Jahnavi and said, “When you're very angry, you can walk round the courtyard, and then come back and tell us what you think.”
Friday: Jahnavi lost another argument with Rafiq. She stamped once, said, “I'm going for my walk,” and left. Ten minutes later she came back. “I still want a turn,” she said. “Okay,” said Rafiq. “Sorry I shouted.”

qa.q: What did Amma suggest Jahnavi could do when she was very angry?
qa.a: She suggested she could walk round the courtyard and then come back and tell them what she thinks.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi probably feeling when she stamped and slammed the door on Monday, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Anger at losing the argument, and probably a need to get away. She may also have felt hurt at being called dramatic.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: Jahnavi used the cooling-off routine: she said she was going for a walk, left, and came back to talk, so the anger did not turn into slamming.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel on Friday when Jahnavi comes back?
qa.a: Probably relieved that the fight did not blow up, and a little sorry, since he apologised for shouting.

grounding: A child stamps and slams the door in anger; a cooling-off walk and return makes a safe boundary.

passage: I'm Seema, and I sat two rows behind Jomon at the class movie about the haunted house. When the music turned creepy, Jomon pulled his knees up and wrapped both arms round himself, chin on his knees. I couldn't tell if he was scared or cold because the air conditioner was on. I leaned forward and whispered, “You okay?” He said, “Just cold. And a bit scared.” I gave him my school sweater to hold. He nodded and held it against his chest for the rest of the film, still watching.

qa.q: Where was Seema sitting compared with Jomon at the movie?
qa.a: Seema was sitting two rows behind Jomon.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he hugged himself, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: A bit scared by the creepy music, and cold too, as he told Seema. Seema could not tell which at first, since both fit.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped?
qa.a: Seema whispered a quiet check-in instead of assuming, and offered her sweater to hold, so Jomon could say how he felt.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about Seema's check-in?
qa.a: Probably comforted that someone noticed without making a fuss. He kept watching, so he did not seem embarrassed.

grounding: A child hugs himself for comfort during a scary film; a quiet check-in beats assuming.

passage:
Monday: at lunch, Jahnavi sat hugging her rag doll to her chest after a quarrel with her friend. Her classmate Rafiq noticed, sat on the next bench and quietly opened his tiffin. He said nothing.
Wednesday: at the bus stop on a cold morning, Jahnavi stood with her arms wrapped round herself. Rafiq asked, “Cold, or something else?” “Both, a bit,” she said. He offered her half his scarf.
Friday: Jahnavi's arms were swinging by her sides. She was telling Rafiq about the quiz, and she laughed.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi hugging at lunch on Monday?
qa.a: She was hugging her rag doll to her chest.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday, and what else might the hugging show?
qa.a: Probably upset after the quarrel with her friend, so she soothed herself with the doll. It may also hint at worry, since she stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that respected Jahnavi at each stage?
qa.a: On Monday he sat nearby and said nothing, and on Wednesday he asked a gentle question and offered half his scarf, so she could answer in her own way.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel about Rafiq's quiet company?
qa.a: Probably comforted and less alone, since by Friday she was laughing and talking to him. She was not pushed to explain.

grounding: Hugging oneself or a soft toy soothes after upset; a quiet check-in helps more than assuming.

passage: On the playground in Manchester, two older boys flicked paper balls at Tariq and called him names. Tariq hunched his shoulders, ducked his head and covered his face with both arms. The boys laughed. Rosa, eating her apple on the bench, watched. The way he curled up didn't look weak or funny to her. It looked frightened, and hurt. She stood up. “Stop it,” she said, loud and steady. The boys shrugged and wandered off. Rosa walked to Tariq. “Come with me,” she said. “Let's tell Ms Hayes.” Tariq lowered his arms and nodded.

qa.q: What did the older boys flick at Tariq?
qa.a: They flicked paper balls at him.

qa.q: What did Rosa read in Tariq's ducked head and covered face, and how sure can she be?
qa.a: She read fear and hurt, not weakness. She cannot be completely sure, but the hunched shoulders and covered face fit that reading.

qa.q: What did Rosa do that was a wise response?
qa.a: She told the boys to stop, went to Tariq and took him to tell a teacher, instead of ignoring it or joining in.

qa.q: How might Tariq feel when Rosa steps in?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, since he lowered his arms and nodded. He may still feel shaky or embarrassed.

grounding: A child recognises that a peer recoiling from a taunt is frightened or hurt, stops it and tells a teacher.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, three older boys at the next table started mocking Anand's haircut, calling out, “Bald eagle!” Anand shrank into his chair, pulled his shoulders up and covered his face with his hands. Tarun, who was standing in the queue with his plate, saw it. He thought about laughing along, like the others, but Anand's hands were shaking. Tarun put his plate down. “That's enough, leave him alone,” he said. Then he sat beside Anand. “Let's tell the warden.” Anand lowered his hands, eyes red. “Okay.”

qa.q: What did the boys call out at Anand?
qa.a: They called out, “Bald eagle!”

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he shrank into his chair and covered his face, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Probably fear and hurt, since his hands were shaking, which is why Tarun stopped and acted. It could also have been embarrassment about the taunt over his haircut.

qa.q: What could Tarun and Anand do next after telling the warden?
qa.a: Stay together, let the warden speak with the older boys, and check in with Anand later so he does not feel alone.

qa.q: How might the older boys see what they did?
qa.a: They may think it was harmless teasing, not noticing Anand's fear. Tarun's words may make them realise it was hurting him.

grounding: A child sees a peer shrink and cover the face during a taunt, stops it and tells an adult.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Aparna, and I sit next to Akash. During the science test he kept scratching his head and rubbing his forehead. I guessed he was stuck, and I felt bad for him. After the test I asked, “Were you stuck?” He laughed. “Not really. My cap made my head itch, and I was sleepy because of the late cricket match. But I was stuck on question five.” So I was partly right and partly wrong. Next time I'll just whisper, “Do you need anything?” without guessing first.

qa.q: What did Akash keep doing during the science test?
qa.a: Akash kept scratching his head and rubbing his forehead.

qa.q: What did Aparna guess Akash was feeling, and how right was that guess?
qa.a: Aparna guessed he was stuck, and was partly right, since he was stuck on question five. His itchy head and sleepiness, from his cap and the late match, also explained the scratching.

qa.q: What would you advise Aparna to do next time?
qa.a: Offer a friendly “Do you need anything?” after the test or quietly, as Aparna plans, without guessing first.

qa.q: How might Akash feel about Aparna's question?
qa.a: Probably amused and glad someone noticed. He answered honestly and laughed, so he does not seem bothered.

grounding: A peer scratching the head during a test may be stuck, itchy or tired; asking beats assuming.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: during the maths test, Arohi scratched her head and rubbed her forehead. Kamal, at the next desk, whispered, “Are you stuck?” “No, just an itch,” she whispered back.
Wednesday: she scratched her head again. Kamal asked after the paper, “Stuck or itchy?” “Stuck on the last one!” she laughed.
Friday: Arohi rubbed her forehead during the spelling test. Kamal just slid his eraser to the side of the desk, in case she needed it. She looked up and smiled, and kept writing.

qa.q: What did Arohi say when Kamal asked if she was stuck on Monday?
qa.a: She said, “No, just an itch.”

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday when she scratched her head, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was probably stuck on the last question, as she said afterwards. On Monday the same gesture was just an itch, so the gesture alone does not tell which.

qa.q: How did Kamal's approach improve between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: He moved from guessing to asking “Stuck or itchy?”, and by Friday he offered a small helpful gesture without interrupting her writing.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel about Kamal's questions?
qa.a: Probably comfortable and supported, since she laughed and smiled. She was not made to feel bad about being stuck.

grounding: Scratching the head may be confusion, an itch or tiredness; a friendly offer beats assuming.

passage: I'm Arnab. When Kalyani presented her project on rivers, she twirled the end of her plait round her finger, tugged her sleeve and straightened her collar twice. Behind me, someone whispered, “She doesn't know it, look at her hair.” I didn't agree. She answered every question the teacher asked, clearly and correctly. I think she was just nervous, since she looks like that every time she stands in front of the class. Afterwards I said, “Nice presentation.” She grinned and let go of her plait.

qa.q: What did Kalyani twirl round her finger?
qa.a: She twirled the end of her plait round her finger.

qa.q: What was Kalyani probably feeling, and what shows that the fidgeting was not proof of not knowing?
qa.a: Probably mild nervousness, since she does it every time she stands in front of the class. She answered every question clearly and correctly, so the twirling did not mean she did not know.

qa.q: What could someone do instead of whispering guesses about her hair?
qa.a: Notice what she actually says and, afterwards, offer a kind word, as Arnab did.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel about Arnab's remark?
qa.a: Probably relieved and pleased, since she grinned and let go of her plait. She may not have known anyone noticed her nerves.

grounding: Twirling hair and tugging clothing are self-comfort acts showing mild tension, not lying.

passage:
Monday: in the class quiz, Pema twirled her hair round her finger before each answer. Varun thought, She doesn't know the answers.
Wednesday: Varun stood to read his poem. His hands went to his collar and tugged it straight, and then his sleeve. He noticed, and thought, That's what nerves do to me.
Friday: Pema twirled her hair again at the quiz. This time Varun did not guess anything. He gave her a small thumbs-up. She smiled, and gave the right answer.

qa.q: What did Pema do with her hair before each answer on Monday?
qa.a: She twirled her hair round her finger before each answer.

qa.q: What did Varun think on Monday about Pema's twirling, and what changed his view?
qa.a: He thought she did not know the answers. On Wednesday he noticed that tugging his own collar and sleeve is what nerves do to him, so the twirling was probably nerves too.

qa.q: What small step did Varun take on Friday?
qa.a: He gave Pema a small thumbs-up and did not guess anything, which was kind and gave her some support.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when Varun gives her a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Probably reassured, since she smiled and gave the right answer. She may not have known he noticed.

grounding: Hair twirling and clothing adjusting are self-comfort acts under mild tension, not signs of not knowing.

passage: Joseph's diary, Tuesday. Reena held my hand while we walked to the bus, like she does with all her friends. Some boys said, “Boyfriend-girlfriend!” That's silly. It's just how we walk together. Sir also patted my back after the quiz and said, “Well done.” That felt nice too, like he was happy for me. But at the gate today I didn't feel like holding hands. I said, “Not today,” and Reena said, “Okay,” and swung her bag. It felt good that I could say that. Mum says if any touch feels off, I can say no and tell her.

qa.q: What did Sir do after the quiz?
qa.a: Sir patted Joseph's back and said, “Well done.”

qa.q: What did Joseph think Reena's hand-holding and Sir's pat meant, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Joseph took them as friendship and reassurance, and the pat felt like Sir was happy for Joseph. Joseph did not treat them as romance.

qa.q: What did Joseph do at the gate, and what does Joseph's mum say?
qa.a: Joseph said “Not today” when hand-holding didn't feel right, and Reena accepted it. Mum says Joseph can say no to any touch that feels off and tell her.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Joseph says “Not today”?
qa.a: Probably fine with it, since she said “Okay” and swung her bag. She may simply have accepted that Joseph wanted a different day.

grounding: Hand-holding and pats among friends show friendship, and a child can refuse any touch that feels off.

passage:
In the village school, Gurpreet Sir gave Madhuri a light pat on the shoulder after her recitation. “Well done.” Madhuri smiled. She and her friend Sarita walked to the pump arm in arm, as always.
Later, a visitor who was leaving the school pinched Madhuri's cheek and laughed. Madhuri frowned and pulled back. Gurpreet Sir noticed. When the visitor had gone, he said, “Did you like that?”
“No,” said Madhuri.
“You can say no to any touch you don't like, and you can always tell me. I'll listen.”

qa.q: Where did Madhuri and Sarita walk arm in arm?
qa.a: They walked to the pump.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel about the pat from Gurpreet Sir compared with the pinch on her cheek?
qa.a: She smiled at the pat, which seemed to reassure her. She frowned and pulled back from the pinch, so she did not like it.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet Sir do that protects Madhuri?
qa.a: He noticed her pulling back, asked if she liked it, and told her she can say no to any touch she doesn't like and tell him.

qa.q: How might the visitor have seen the cheek pinch?
qa.a: Possibly as a friendly gesture, without noticing that Madhuri did not like it. That is why saying no matters.

grounding: Pats and hand-holding among friends show warmth; unwanted touch can be refused and reported.

passage: Sports day was so loud that nobody could hear anything. Tenzin crossed the line first in the relay, and his teammate Binita jumped up with her palm raised. He slapped it in a high-five, both laughing. The chief guest came down to the track and held out a hand. “Well run.” Tenzin shook it, politely, looking her in the eye. Then he saw Binita standing a little apart. She didn't like being touched by strangers. When another teammate held up a hand to her, she gave a big wave instead. The teammate waved back, grinning, and the noise closed over all of them.

qa.q: Who crossed the line first in the relay?
qa.a: Tenzin crossed the line first.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he slapped Binita's high-five, and what did the handshake show?
qa.a: He was probably excited and proud of his run. The handshake with the chief guest showed politeness and respect, in a more formal moment.

qa.q: What could Binita do when she prefers not to touch someone?
qa.a: Offer a wave instead, as she did, which still shows warmth.

qa.q: How might the other teammate feel when Binita waves rather than high-fives?
qa.a: Probably fine with it, since the teammate waved back grinning. The teammate may see the wave as a friendly greeting in its own right.

grounding: High-five, handshake and a wave each carry warmth; a child who prefers not to touch can wave.

passage:
At the school gate in the morning, Shankar held out a fist and Lokesh bumped it. “Ready for the test?” “Nope,” said Lokesh. “But ready for lunch.” They grinned.
Inside, the visiting principal stood in the corridor, and Shankar stepped forward to shake her hand. “Good morning, ma'am. Welcome to our school.” She smiled. Lokesh hung back. He was shy about touch with people he didn't know, so he joined his palms and said, “Namaste, ma'am.”
She returned the namaste. “Lovely to meet you.” Lokesh let out a breath.

qa.q: What did Lokesh say when Shankar asked if he was ready for the test?
qa.a: He said, “Nope. But ready for lunch.”

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he hung back, and what did he do about it?
qa.a: He was shy about touching someone he did not know, so he chose a namaste instead of a handshake. He seemed relieved when she returned it.

qa.q: What does this show about greeting choices?
qa.a: A child can pick a warm, respectful greeting that suits him, such as a namaste, wave or fist bump, and that is enough.

qa.q: How might the visiting principal see Lokesh's namaste?
qa.a: As a polite and warm greeting, since she returned it and said it was lovely to meet him.

grounding: Fist bump, handshake and namaste all show warmth; a child who prefers not to touch can offer another greeting.

passage:
“Aadhya moved to another table today,” said Yash, pushing his rice around his plate.
“Did you two argue?” asked Mummy.
“About who gets to be science partner.”
“What do you think her moving means?”
“Maybe she's angry. Or hurt.” Yash frowned. “Or maybe she just wants space.”
“Could be any of those. What might help?”
“Not chasing her, I guess. I could leave a note.”
“Good idea.”
He tore a page from his notebook. “Sorry about the science thing. Sit with me if you like.” He smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Yash and Aadhya argue about?
qa.a: They argued about who gets to be science partner.

qa.q: What does Yash think Aadhya's move to another table might mean?
qa.a: That she might be angry or hurt, or might just want space. He does not decide which, since a move could mean any of those.

qa.q: What could help repair the friendship?
qa.a: A kind note and an open invitation, as Yash writes, and not chasing or pushing her, so Aadhya can come back in her own time.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when she finds the note?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved and a bit touched that Yash respected her space. She may still need time before she sits with him.

grounding: A friend moves to another table after an argument; a kind note repairs more than pushing.

passage: After Rehana and I argued about the rules of the game, she picked up her lunch box and moved to the next table. I felt my stomach drop. I thought she hated me. I wanted to run over, but Mum had told me that sometimes a friend just needs space. So I wrote a note and slipped it into her bag: “I'm sorry I shouted. You can sit with me whenever you want. Jyoti.” The next day she came and sat down. She said, “I was hurt, but I also needed some time to cool down.” I was glad I hadn't chased her.

qa.q: Where did Rehana move after the argument?
qa.a: She moved to the next table with her lunch box.

qa.q: What did Jyoti think Rehana's move meant, and what did Rehana say later?
qa.a: At first Jyoti thought Rehana hated them. Rehana said she was hurt and also needed time to cool down, so it was both hurt and a need for space.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Jyoti left a kind note with an open invitation instead of chasing, which gave Rehana space and a way back.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt finding the note in her bag?
qa.a: Probably touched and relieved that Jyoti said sorry without pushing. It made it easier to come back the next day.

grounding: A friend moves away after an argument, which may mean hurt or a need for space; a kind note helps.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage:
“Psst, Urmila,” whispered Sumit, leaning across the desk. “Guess what happened to Sir's chair yesterday.” Urmila leaned in, eyes wide. Behind them, Ravi stopped writing and stared at his book. His shoulders had sunk a little.
Urmila noticed. She sat back. “Ravi, come listen. Sumit's got a funny story.”
“It's not that funny,” said Sumit, but he shifted over. “Okay, listen.” He told it out loud, and all three of them laughed.
Ravi grinned. “That's really funny.”

qa.q: Who leaned across the desk to whisper to Urmila?
qa.a: Sumit leaned across the desk to whisper.

qa.q: What did Sumit's leaning in and whispering show, and how might Ravi have felt?
qa.a: It showed trust and a wish to share, but Ravi's sinking shoulders and stare at his book suggest he felt left out. He might also just have been focusing on his work.

qa.q: What did Urmila do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed Ravi and invited him to listen, so the story became a shared one and nobody was left out.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit had kept whispering?
qa.a: Ravi might have felt excluded and stayed quiet, and Urmila might have felt caught between them.

grounding: Leaning in to whisper signals trust and inclusion, and those left out may feel excluded; including them helps.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage: I'm Joseph. At lunch I leaned toward Reena to show her a funny picture on my dad's phone. We both laughed so hard we had to hold our stomachs. Across the table Kabir's face went still, and he started stirring his dal. I realised he couldn't see and he hadn't been asked. I felt a bit bad. So I turned the screen so he could see it too. “Sorry, Kabir, look!” He laughed as well, and the stirring stopped. I want to remember that leaning in together feels great for the two people, but the others notice.

qa.q: What did Joseph show Reena on his dad's phone?
qa.a: Joseph showed Reena a funny picture.

qa.q: What was Kabir probably feeling when his face went still and he stirred his dal, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably left out, since he could not see the picture and had not been asked. It might also just have been that he was focused on his lunch.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that repaired the moment?
qa.a: Joseph noticed Kabir, turned the screen so he could see it and said sorry, so all three could share the joke.

qa.q: How might Reena feel about Joseph turning the screen?
qa.a: Probably happy to share, since she was already laughing with Joseph. She may not have noticed Kabir until Joseph did.

grounding: Leaning close to share signals trust; those left out may feel excluded and including them is kind.

passage: In art class, Sir held up his own cow drawing, which looked a lot like a table. “Behold, my masterpiece!” he said, and the whole class laughed, including Sir. Later, when Chaitanya knocked over the water jar and it splashed across the floor, a few children laughed too. But Chaitanya didn't laugh. He stared at his shoes, his ears red. Pradeep felt the two kinds of laughter were not the same. The first had made Sir look happy. The second made Chaitanya look small. Pradeep didn't join in. He picked up a cloth and said, “I'll help.”

qa.q: What did Sir's cow drawing look like?
qa.a: It looked a lot like a table.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya probably feeling when the children laughed and he stared at his shoes, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and hurt, since his ears went red and he did not laugh. He might also have been worried about the mess.

qa.q: How did the two kinds of laughter differ, and what did Pradeep do?
qa.a: Sir laughed with everyone at a joke he made on himself, while some children laughed at Chaitanya's mistake. Pradeep did not join in and helped clean up instead.

qa.q: How might Sir see the first laughter?
qa.a: As friendly and shared, since he was laughing with the class. He might not have noticed the second kind if he was looking at the board.

grounding: Laughing with someone is friendly and includes them; laughing at someone's mistake can hurt.

passage: I'm Parveen. At assembly, Ujjwal read the notice in a funny cartoon voice, and the whole hall laughed. He grinned and bowed a bit. That was laughing with him, because he had made the joke. An hour later, during the races, his big borrowed shoe flew off and a few boys laughed. This time Ujjwal did not grin. He hopped over and looked at the ground. I wasn't sure what he felt, maybe embarrassed, maybe he was just annoyed. I picked up the shoe and said, “Here.” He said thanks, quietly, and we jogged back together.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal read in a cartoon voice?
qa.a: He read the notice in a cartoon voice at assembly.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal seem to feel about the two kinds of laughter, and how sure can Parveen be?
qa.a: He grinned at the first, which he had invited, and did not grin at the second, so he probably felt embarrassed by it. Parveen admits not being sure; he might also have been annoyed.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that was a good response to laughter at Ujjwal's mistake?
qa.a: Parveen did not join the laughing, picked up the shoe and offered it, then jogged back with Ujjwal.

qa.q: How might the boys who laughed see what happened?
qa.a: They might have thought it was just funny, not noticing Ujjwal did not enjoy it. Seeing Parveen help may make them think again.

grounding: Laughing with a person differs from laughing at a mistake; an observer notices and helps.
